title: The Squeeze — a shut strait, a gold record, and a number that prints tonight

turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Wednesday, the twelfth of August. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Three things this morning. One — Tehran and Muscat say a deal on the Strait of Hormuz is very close. We'll explain why, on the published terms, close actually means closed.

Two — the loudest inflation number of the month lands tonight, Singapore time. And here's the thing… oil has already written the story. Gold went through four thousand four hundred US dollars while everyone was watching the diplomats.
And three — the screen-free craft where nothing you make is yours until it survives two trips through a kiln. Theo has been emotionally compromised by a lump of clay.
[laughs] I have opinions about centering. Genuine opinions. Stay with us.
So. The strait. Month six of the closure, and this week Iranian and Omani officials keep using the same two words — very close.
Which sounds like a reopening.

Read the terms Tehran's own state media are publishing, and it is the opposite of open water. A lane that bars all American and Israeli-linked vessels. Fines for violators of up to a fifth of the cargo's value. And a temporary route that only runs until a replacement is negotiated for the old traffic separation scheme.
Hang on — a fifth of the cargo. So you sail through, and if they decide you're on the wrong list, they take twenty per cent of everything you're carrying?
That's the published term. And Iran's foreign minister says reopening stays, quote, subject to other conditions — including compensation from the United States for an alleged breach back in June.
So the toll booth is already built. They're just arguing about the price list.

That's exactly the desk's line — a reopening you cannot sail is a toll booth with a press release. And as we went to print, not one routine commercial transit had resumed. Last issue's still-no-ship is now settled fact.
Okay, but here's what I find genuinely interesting — the market has stopped waiting. It's not holding its breath for the diplomats anymore.

No. The trade has rerouted around the politics. Traffic is running on the workaround corridors — Jask to Khasab, and around Musandam — and the shipping-risk desks count the operator roster on those routes up roughly threefold since February.
Threefold. That's owners pricing a managed closure. Not a reopening.

And the cleanest read of all sits in the oil price. Brent firmed toward eighty-eight US dollars this week — helped along by a reported Houthi strike on a Saudi Aramco refinery. One report, worth flagging.
So a supply scare on top of a supply scare.
War-risk premiums stay high, and the insurance desks are telling anyone who asks — nobody books a Gulf transit on a communiqué.
Now, Oman. They're hosting the talks. What's their read?
Constructive, they say — but with a warning that continuing Iranian attacks on shipping threaten the whole thing. And Tehran's framing, via state media, is pure sovereignty. Our water, our terms.
And the sceptic's box on this one?
That very close is a posture, not a timetable. A corridor priced by one side, barred to two navies, and conditioned on a payment the other side calls extortion — that isn't a thaw.
It's a chokepoint learning to charge rent.
That's the sentence. Hold that thought, because the money story tonight flows straight out of it.
Right — the money block. Walk me backwards through the week, because the desk says it all starts at that chokepoint.

It does. Shut strait, burning refinery — reported — and oil does what oil does with a supply scare. Brent toward eighty-eight. Higher energy feeds straight into inflation expectations, so the US ten-year yield backed up to a one-month high, near four point seven per cent.
The market leaning back toward a Fed that holds higher for longer.

Dollar steady, the dollar index around ninety-nine point seven. And then the tell — gold pushed through four thousand four hundred US dollars to a multi-month high. Despite rising yields, which usually cap it.
Which is weird, right? Explain the machinery there, because that combination matters.

Rising yields normally hurt gold — it pays no interest, so higher real yields make it expensive to hold. When gold rips anyway, the inflation-and-haven bid is overpowering that headwind. That's the signature of an inflation scare — not a growth scare.
And bitcoin, the high-beta read on all this, softened — about sixty-four thousand US dollars. Traders de-risking into the print.

Which brings us to tonight. July's US inflation number prints at eight-thirty in the morning New York time — which is tonight for us, after the edition went to bed. So the book treats it honestly as awaiting.
Two paths. Give me both.

A hot number, on top of an oil scare, hardens higher-for-longer, firms the dollar, and pressures an equity tape already at records and leaning on air. A soft number lets that yield spike unwind fast — and the trade most exposed to a soft surprise is the gold sitting at records.
Mm. And the desk's standing line — market explanation, not investment advice.
Always. Now — Singapore, because the local story this week is the mirror image of a squeeze. It's a surplus.
A widening one. Second-quarter growth came in at five point seven per cent year on year. Exports up about a fifth on the year in June. The Government keeps being handed room it hasn't spent.

So the argument has moved. It's no longer whether Singapore can afford to help stretched households — it's how, and whether it gets written into law. The Workers' Party tabled its motion on the fourth of August. Pritam Singh's two demands — legislate mandatory retrenchment benefits, and give a clearer account of the spending as the surplus widens.

And that lands two days after the Prime Minister's National Day message — families stretched between kids, ageing parents and work, the A I job anxiety named out loud, and a promised major review of family support.

Details deferred to the Rally — the twenty-third of August, ITE College Central. That's where the choice becomes concrete. Recurring family relief — leave, childcare-fee caps, a standing top-up — or bankable one-offs that flatter a Budget and fade.
And the bar the desk sets for that evening is a good one. Prior rounds of vouchers haven't moved a fertility rate near zero point nine seven. So the test on the twenty-third…
…is a number that changes a behaviour, not a headline that soothes one. Capacity is not the excuse. Intent is the test.
Property, briefly — because the record headlines and the real signal are pointing in different directions again.

June set a record — a hundred and eighty-eight million-dollar flats. But the resale index fell for a second straight quarter. And July resale volume jumped by a quarter to about two thousand six hundred and sixty — a high for the year — after the private-downgrader wait-out was lifted.
So records at the top, softness underneath. And the state is quietly setting the ceiling.

Two big confirmed-list sites on the tender block. The one to watch — New Upper Changi Road, right against Bedok MRT, up to about one thousand and ten units, tender closing at noon on the first of September. Consultants pencil top bids around one thousand four hundred Singapore dollars per square foot of buildable area.
And the logic — every future fringe launch is a cap on the last one's upside. Supply is the quiet story that matters.
The desk's read for an owner is unromantic — the million-dollar record is a top-decile event, not a floor under a heartland flat. Not investment advice.
Technology. And I love this one, because it's about the difference between a border and a login.

Washington finally named the back door. You can't buy a restricted Nvidia card into China — but you can rent one by the hour in Bangkok or Kuala Lumpur. And Chinese A I firms have been doing exactly that.
Legally. That's the wild part.

At present, yes. Around the seventh of August, reporting said the Commerce Department's export arm is systematically reviewing how Chinese firms reach restricted chips offshore — and it's building two lists. Countries running black-market physical diversion, and countries where the silicon gets tapped remotely.
Named in scope — Alibaba, Tencent, ByteDance, Moonshot. And there's a House-passed bill, the Remote Access Security Act, that would make the rental itself illegal. But it hasn't cleared the Senate.
So the honest read is that this is naming, not yet enforcing. A map of the back door, published to deter the traffic through it.
Export controls stop a chip crossing a border. They do not stop a login. That line's going to age well.
The desk's sceptic cuts the other way, though — Nvidia has already lost effectively its whole China shipment share, and policing overseas rental is near-unenforceable without allies on board.

Meanwhile the home-lab page is having a very good week. Meta put out a thirty-billion-parameter model, open licence, sized so it actually fits on a serious home graphics card — built not to be a chatbot, but for always-on local agents. Tool use, local coding, judging other models' output.

Behind your own firewall — the one job a rented cloud model can't do. And the page's party trick — a hundred-and-twenty-billion-parameter open model running on a single card that can't physically hold it, because only about five billion parameters fire per token, and the rest spill into system memory.
Sparsity, not capacity. That's how a home rig reaches a hundred-billion-class model at all. [excited] I find that genuinely thrilling.

The Kit will calm you down. The Insta three-sixty X six — the camera this desk told everyone to wait on — went on sale on our cover date. Six hundred and ninety-nine US dollars. A real hundred-and-fifty-dollar jump on the X five.
And the verdict changed how much?

Not at all. On paper it's the class leader — dual one-inch-class sensors, eight-K at fifty frames, a bigger battery. But at filing there is no independent lab review anywhere, because the camera is a day old. Day one is a bet.
And the reader who waits a fortnight for the lab numbers pays… exactly the same price, and carries none of the risk of being the test unit.
The wait ended. The counsel didn't.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every single morning with this.
The line is the line. Today — studio pottery. Clay, spun on a wheel, braced into shape with your hands. And the hook is one silent moment. Centering.
Describe it, since you've clearly rehearsed.

You lean a wet, wobbling lump onto a spinning wheel, brace your arms against your body, and press — and there's an instant where the whole thing suddenly goes still and true under your palms. Every potter names that moment as the gateway drug. It's meditative, it's tactile, and there is no screen anywhere.
And then reality arrives.

Then reality arrives. Because the wheel is maybe a tenth of this craft. Every piece has to travel the whole pipeline — thrown, trimmed leather-hard, dried to bone-dry, a first bisque firing, then glazed, then a second, hotter firing. Up to one thousand three hundred degrees. You do not own the result until it survives both fires.
Two chances for the kiln to eat your work.

And the community treats that as the point. A kiln opening is a communal lottery — everyone crowding round to see what lived. There's even a named villain — the S-crack. A crack in the base you caused weeks earlier by not compressing the clay, and the kiln just… reveals it.
The boom is real, though. This isn't nostalgia.

It's booming for a reason a desk-worker will recognise instantly — it was framed this year as the anti-digital hobby. Wellness-driven, tactile, a counterweight to knowledge work. Studios now count corporate-wellness bookings and universities as actual revenue lines.
Where do people gather?

Reddit's the town square — a big beginner-friendly pottery sub that's wall-to-wall wheel advice and what-went-wrong firing photos, and a more sculptural ceramics sub of about a hundred and sixty-four thousand. The real front door is YouTube — Florian Gadsby, one point eight million subscribers of meditative porcelain. And the authority voice is Ceramic Arts Network, where the eternal argument is electric versus gas versus wood firing.
Now the part our reader actually asks — the gear, read buy-once.

Blunt answer. Skip the cheap tabletop wheels — the consensus is they stall the moment you lean on the clay. The wheel worth buying once is the quietest direct-drive on the market, about one thousand eight hundred and fifty dollars. But the kiln — the kiln is a decision you make with an electrician, not a shopping cart. Serious ones run two and a half to four thousand, and most apartments simply can't host one. Power, and venting.
Which reframes the whole hobby.

It's a membership hobby in practice, and that's the sceptic's case too — most people should never buy a kiln at all. Rent the fire. In Singapore that's actually a gift — Mud Rock for serious courses, Goodman's studios… and Thow Kwang, an actual wood-fired dragon kiln, where a taster is about eighty Singapore dollars.
A dragon kiln. In Jurong.

A multi-day, shift-stoked, communal firing marathon. [curious] And the honest first ninety days invert the shopping instinct entirely — lurk first, watch Gadsby end to end so you understand the pipeline, take a real class… and buy nothing.
The cutting edge?

A smart kiln controller that fires the kiln from your phone, with the cone chart baked into the firmware. Verdict — promising, and one year old, so too new to judge. The desk held it. Which I respect.
The two-fire craft. And if that grabbed you, the book gives it three full pages, gear tables and all.
Culture corner. Friday's music story is a split-screen.

Karol G dropped her sixth album on the seventh — an atmospheric heartbreak record carrying her first-ever official Drake collaboration, plus a Bruno Mars feature. Reviews generally positive — a superstar moment, said one — with a persistent grumble that it's too mild for the reggaetón crowd that made her.
And the quieter record out the same day is the one the critics actually rated higher. Ravyn Lenae — Blue Island. A Metacritic of seventy-eight, the week's real find by the reviews.
The recurring culture-desk lesson — the biggest launch and the best-reviewed one are rarely the same record.

And Friday belongs to Phoebe Bridgers. Lost Weekend — sixteen tracks, her first solo album since Punisher — arriving with advance acclaim the public hasn't heard a note of. Filed at a score it hasn't yet had to defend.

The Family Desk this week is one worth every parent's two minutes. The American pediatrics academy retired its hours-per-day screen rule this year — moving to what a child is doing and how, over how long.

But the sharper finding underneath — a meta-analysis of a hundred and fifty-three longitudinal studies found the social-media harm signal is not flat across childhood. It concentrates in early adolescence — the eleven-to-thirteen band — and runs stronger in girls.
So the years around eleven are when the unglamorous work matters most. General guidance, not medical advice — but a genuinely useful map.

Fitness gives us the smallest dose on record. Exercise snacks — bouts of five minutes or less, a couple of times a day. A pooled analysis of eleven trials found they measurably raised V O two max at volumes as low as about four and a half minutes a week.
Four and a half minutes. A week. The no-time excuse is officially dead — it fits in a stairwell.
Caveat kept — it helped the previously inactive most. And why care — V O two max is among the strongest predictors of longevity there is.

One diary item to set an alarm for — BIGBANG's return, one night at the National Stadium in October, general sale Thursday at ten. And behind it a Kallang autumn that stacks Post Malone, the Weeknd, and Singapore's first-ever Formula One Sprint into six weeks.
And then the long read. Theo — tell it slowly, because this one earns it.

In March, a thirty-four-year-old Korean software developer named Choi Sung-soo lost his job in an A I restructuring. Living on severance, he capped his own food budget at ten thousand won a day — about seven US dollars. And then he built a tool for everyone else doing the same.
A crowdsourced map of every restaurant serving a meal under that line.

The Beggar Map, he calls it. One point three million visitors within a month. More than two and a half thousand places on it now — running, in his own dry phrase, on the collective intelligence and strict evaluation of beggars.
And the Koreans already have a name for the culture around it.

Jjantech — stingy, plus tech. Thrift reframed as a competitive skill. A strategy with a scoreboard. And the desk's argument is that this is the first consumer subculture visibly shaped by white-collar A I displacement — the convenience store as a generation's default kitchen.
The recursion is the story in miniature. The tool for surviving the A I layoffs was itself born from one.

[pause] What stays with me is the dignity of it. He didn't write a manifesto. He made the spreadsheet everyone needed, and a million people showed up in a month. When the big papers get round to naming Korea's jjantech underclass — it will already have a name, a scoreboard, and two and a half thousand restaurants.
Downturns don't announce themselves in the data first. They show up in how people eat.
That's the hour — well, the twenty minutes.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all. Tonight's inflation print gets its verdict in tomorrow's edition.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
